results.summary: This design consists of four inverters, where inputs zero to three pass directly to the corresponding outputs and the remaining inputs are inverted. It is intended to be exercised by toggling the input switches, requiring no external hardware. The documentation is very thin and partly garbled, so the exact mapping of the remaining input and output pins is not fully clear. It appears to be a simple logic experiment or class exercise rather than a complete functional block.

This design decodes a four-bit binary value into the seven-segment control signals needed to show the corresponding decimal digit. Inputs zero through three represent the binary number, and the outputs drive a common seven-segment display. No external hardware other than the display itself is required, and it is a straightforward educational decoder design.

This design is an eight-bit buffer that takes four-bit inputs and displays the loaded value. No external hardware is required, and the documentation describes it as a test workshop exercise. Flip switch N, where N is switch 1-8, and the corresponding digit will appear on the display.

This design lights the digit corresponding to whichever of the eight input switches is active, mapping switch one to digit one through switch eight to digit eight. It is tested by flipping individual switches and checking that the matching digit appears on the seven-segment display. The documentation is sparse but the intended behavior is clear. No external hardware is required beyond the display.

This design chains four flip-flops together and shifts the state of input in0 through them, driving a seven-segment display. It is tested by toggling the in0 switch and watching the shifted state appear on the display or LEDs. Wire up the outputs to a 7-segment display, and send a ON signal on IN0.

This project is described as a simple logic gate with two inputs and two outputs. The documentation only says 'Testing' for both how it works and how to test it, and it names no specific gate function. The external hardware section is left as the default placeholder text, giving no real information. The documentation is extremely thin and partly unreliable, so the design cannot be clearly characterised.

This design claims that, after a very long delay, it will render the letter V, though the exact output encoding is not specified. The external hardware section is left as the default placeholder text, giving no real information. The documentation is extremely thin and partly unreliable, so the design cannot be clearly characterised.

This design adds two four-bit binary numbers and drives the five-bit sum onto the outputs. Inputs zero through three carry number A and inputs four through seven carry number B, with the least significant bits at zero and four respectively; the output sum also has its least significant bit at output zero. External hardware consists of eight input switches and five output LEDs, and the documentation is clear about the encoding despite being a simple class exercise.

This design is a parity detector that computes the parity of the eight input bits and drives an LED to indicate odd or even parity. It is tested by setting the input switches and observing the LED state. No external hardware is required beyond the LED. The documentation is sparse but the intent is clear.
